content: 1. Regulatory and policy frameworks, along with political, sociocultural, institutional, and economic factors, play a significant role in shaping health interventions and decision-making processes. 2. Evidence-to-decision tables are structured frameworks designed to assist individuals in making and utilizing evidence-informed recommendations and decisions. Their primary purpose is to enable decision-makers to systematically and transparently incorporate evidence into their processes. 3. In the context of WHO guidelines, evidence-to-decision frameworks provide members of the Guideline Development Group (GDG) with a comparative analysis of the advantages and disadvantages of the interventions under consideration. They ensure that all relevant criteria for decision-making are addressed, offer concise summaries of the best available evidence for each criterion, and help structure and document discussions. These frameworks also identify reasons for disagreements, ensuring transparency in the decision-making process. 4. Family planning enables individuals to achieve their desired number of children and determine the spacing of pregnancies. This is accomplished through the use of contraceptive methods and the treatment of infertility. 5. Fertility refers to the biological capacity to establish a clinical pregnancy. It is influenced by various factors, including environmental and workplace conditions, as well as societal and cultural considerations that affect reproductive family planning options. 6. Fertility care encompasses interventions aimed at increasing fertility awareness, providing support, and managing fertility to help individuals and couples achieve their reproductive goals. 7. Gender equality ensures that diverse groups of women and men have equal opportunities to access and control social, economic, and political resources, including legal protections such as health services, education, and voting rights. Achieving gender equality often requires targeted measures to support groups with limited access to these resources. 8. Gender equity recognizes the differing needs, preferences, and interests of individuals based on their gender. It may involve providing different treatments to ensure equal opportunities, addressing the realities of people’s lives, and reducing gender-based health inequities. 9. Gender-responsive policies and programs actively address gender norms, roles, and inequalities, implementing measures to mitigate their harmful effects. 10. Harm or social harm refers to any intentional or unintentional act that causes physical, economic, emotional, or psychosocial injury or distress, whether inflicted by another person, oneself, or an institution. 11. A health intervention is any action performed for, with, or on behalf of an individual or population to assess, improve, maintain, promote, or modify health, functioning, or health conditions. These interventions can include diagnostic, medical, surgical, mental health, primary care, rehabilitation, traditional medicine, and public health measures. 12. HIV self-testing involves an individual collecting their own specimen (oral fluid or blood), performing a test, and interpreting the result, often in a private setting, either alone or with a trusted person. 13. HIV status refers to the final interpretation of a person’s disease state based on testing results. It may be reported as HIV-positive, HIV-negative, or HIV-inconclusive. 14. HPV self-sampling allows individuals to collect their own (cervico-)vaginal sample using a kit, which is then sent to a laboratory for analysis. While it does not diagnose cervical (pre-)cancer, it identifies individuals at higher risk of HPV infection. 15. Human rights are legal guarantees universally applicable to all individuals, protecting against actions that interfere with fundamental freedoms and human dignity. Governments are obligated to establish systems and procedures that enable people to enjoy their guaranteed rights. 16. Infertility is a disease characterized by the inability to establish a clinical pregnancy after 12 months of regular, unprotected sexual intercourse or due to an impairment in reproductive capacity. Fertility interventions may be initiated earlier based on medical history, age, physical findings, and diagnostic testing. 17. Informed decision-making respects individual dignity and autonomy, allowing people to make reproductive choices freely and with comprehensive information, counseling, and support. This principle is central to medical ethics and human rights law. 18. Intersectionality examines how gender interacts with other factors such as race, ethnicity, age, class, geographic location, gender identity, and sexual orientation. It acknowledges that unequal gender power relations intersect with other social and economic inequalities, contributing to health inequities. 19. Intimate partner violence includes behaviors within an intimate relationship that cause physical, psychological, or sexual harm, such as physical violence, sexual violence, emotional abuse, and controlling behaviors. 20. Key populations are groups at increased risk of HIV due to specific high-risk behaviors, regardless of the epidemic type or local context. These include men who have sex with men, people who inject drugs, individuals in prisons or closed settings, sex workers, and transgender people. 21. Lay health workers are individuals trained to perform health-care delivery functions but lack formal professional or para-professional certification or relevant tertiary education degrees. 22. Medically assisted reproduction involves various interventions, procedures, surgeries, and technologies to address fertility impairments and infertility. These include ovulation induction, ovarian stimulation, assisted reproductive technology procedures, uterine transplantation, and various forms of insemination. 23. mHealth refers to the use of mobile and wireless technologies to support health-sector objectives as part of eHealth. 24. Non-discrimination is a human rights principle requiring states to ensure that human rights are exercised without discrimination based on race, color, sex, language, religion, political opinion, national or social origin, property, birth, or other statuses such as disability, marital status, health status, or sexual orientation. 25. Participation ensures that individuals have the right to be actively involved in decisions that directly affect them, including the design, implementation, and monitoring of health interventions. This principle is reaffirmed in international human rights law and conventions. 26. Patient engagement promotes active involvement of patients and the public in health care and decision-making processes. It emphasizes the importance of preserving trust between clinicians and patients and includes patient participation in designing patient-centered systems. 27. Patient experience encompasses the range of interactions patients have with the health-care system, including care from health plans, doctors, nurses, and staff. It includes aspects of care delivery that patients value, such as timely appointments, accessible information, and effective communication. 28. Patient safety refers to the absence of preventable harm to patients during health care and the reduction of risks associated with care to an acceptable minimum, considering current knowledge, resources, and context. 29. People-centeredness involves providing care that respects and responds to individual preferences, needs, and values, ensuring that patient values guide all clinical decisions. 30. Point-of-care testing allows diagnostic tests to be conducted near the patient, with results available during the same visit and used immediately for care and referral. 31. Pregnancy is the state of reproduction beginning with the implantation of an embryo in the uterus and ending with the complete expulsion or extraction of all products of implantation. 32. Privacy and confidentiality ensure that individuals accessing health information and services are protected from interference with their privacy and that health workers maintain the confidentiality of medical information. 33. Psychosocial support addresses the psychological and physical needs of individuals in specific situations, helping them accept and cope with their circumstances. 34. Quality in health care refers to the degree to which services increase the likelihood of desired health outcomes and align with current professional knowledge. It includes skilled personnel, scientifically approved drugs, safe water, and adequate sanitation. 35. Quality assurance is a component of quality management that provides confidence to stakeholders that quality requirements will be met. 36. Self-administration refers to individuals administering pharmacological substances or biomedical interventions to themselves.
